source.author: stat
source.text: iamque super ripas utroque exstantior ibat aggere, iam medium modo qui superaverat amnem Hippomedon intactus aquis umerosque manusque, miratur crevisse vadum seseque minorem, hinc atque hinc tumidi fluctus animosaque surgit tempestas instar pelagi, cum Pliadas haurit aut nigrum trepidis impingit Oriona nautis, non secus aequoreo iactat Teumesius amnis Hippomedonta salo, semperque umbone sinistro tollitur et clipeum nigrante supervenit aestu spumeus assultans, fractaque refunditur unda et cumulo maiore redit; nec mole liquenti contentus carpit putres servantia ripas arbusta annosasque trabes eiectaque fundo saxa rotat, stat pugna impar amnisque virique, indignante deo; nec enim dat terga nec ullis frangitur ille minis, venientesque obvius undas intrat et obiecta dispellit flumina parma, stant terra fugiente gradus, et poplite tenso lubrica saxa tenet, genibusque obnixus et haerens subruta fallaci servat vestigia limo, sic etiam increpitans:
source.text_original: iamque super ripas utroque exstantior ibat / aggere, iam medium modo qui superaverat amnem / Hippomedon intactus aquis umerosque manusque, / miratur crevisse vadum seseque minorem, / hinc atque hinc tumidi fluctus animosaque surgit / tempestas instar pelagi, cum Pliadas haurit / aut nigrum trepidis impingit Oriona nautis, / non secus aequoreo iactat Teumesius amnis / Hippomedonta salo, semperque umbone sinistro / tollitur et clipeum nigrante supervenit aestu / spumeus assultans, fractaque refunditur unda / et cumulo maiore redit; nec mole liquenti / contentus carpit putres servantia ripas / arbusta annosasque trabes eiectaque fundo / saxa rotat, stat pugna impar amnisque virique, / indignante deo; nec enim dat terga nec ullis / frangitur ille minis, venientesque obvius undas / intrat et obiecta dispellit flumina parma, / stant terra fugiente gradus, et poplite tenso / lubrica saxa tenet, genibusque obnixus et haerens / subruta fallaci servat vestigia limo, / sic etiam increpitans:
source.text_english: And now, having gone over the banks on a ridge rising higher on either side, Hippomedon, who had just crossed the middle of the stream intact in the water, marvels that the ford has grown and that he himself seems smaller. On this side and that the swollen waves rise up, and the storm mounts with spirit like the sea, when it swallows the Pleiades or hurls black Orion at terrified sailors. Even so the Teumesian river tosses Hippomedon in the sea-like flood, and always, lifted on the left-hand boss of his shield, he rises and, foaming, surges over the shield, with the dark flood pressing on him; and, when the wave breaks, it flows back and returns in a larger mass. Nor content with its watery bulk does it pluck away the rotten shrubs that hold the banks, and the ancient beams, and roll the stones torn from the bottom. The struggle stands unequal, river and man, while the god is angered. For he neither turns his back nor is broken by any threats, but goes straight into the waves as they come and scatters the waters opposed against him with his shield; with the ground fleeing beneath him, his steps stand firm, and with tense knee he holds the slippery stones, and, bracing himself on his knees and clinging on, he preserves his footing on the undermined mud despite its treachery, thus even shouting in defiance:

reuse.author: val
reuse.text: At ducis imperiis Minyae monituque frequentes puppem umeris subeunt et tento poplite proni decurrunt intrantque fretum.
reuse.text_original: At ducis imperiis Minyae monituque frequentes / puppem umeris subeunt et tento poplite proni / decurrunt intrantque fretum.
reuse.text_english: But at the commander’s orders and under his urging, the many Minyae take up the ship on their shoulders and, with bent knees, run downhill and enter the strait.
